title: "CyberTrust AI v2: A Multi-Agent Adversarial Framework for Automated Smart Contract Exploit Synthesis and Economic Invariant Verification"
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
authors: Yash Mandaviya
abstract: Paper I in this series introduced CyberTrust AI, a production-deployed framework applying a single-pass large language model (LLM) audit to detect, classify, and remediate Solidity smart contract vulnerabilities, demonstrating a detection advantage over rule-based static analysis on indirect reentrancy and access-control logic patterns. This paper, Volume II, presents CyberTrust AI v2, which extends the single-pass architecture into a multi-agent, adversarial, and generative security analysis pipeline comprising four new subsystems: (1) a Multi-Agent Audit Council, in which four narrowly-scoped specialist agents (reentrancy, access control, economic/tokenomics, and gas/logic) analyze a contract in parallel and a Lead Auditor agent synthesizes their findings into a unified trust score and consensus assessment; (2) an Adversarial Red Team / Blue Team simulation that produces a structured, multi-round attack-and-defense transcript culminating in a final severity rating; (3) an Automated Exploit Proof-of-Concept generator that produces complete, runnable Foundry test files demonstrating identified vulnerabilities end-to-end; and (4) an Economic Invariant Extraction and Fuzz Test Generator that derives protocol-level invariants (e.g., solvency, conservation of recorded balances) and emits Foundry invariant test suites targeting them. We additionally describe the system's transition from a stateless demonstration tool to a multi-tenant SaaS platform, including authentication, tiered usage limits, and per-route cost-control architecture. We present a case study evaluation on two contracts — a reentrancy/access-control contract carried over from Paper I for continuity, and a new staking vault contract exercising the invariant-checking pipeline — in which the new subsystems are applied using their exact production system prompts. The case study surfaces a notable methodological finding: the Audit Council's narrative severity synthesis rates the staking vault “Grade C / NFT-eligible” (trust score 74/100) despite containing a permanent, unrecoverable accounting desynchronization, while the Invariant Checker's generated fuzz test reduces this same defect to a concrete two-call counterexample — illustrating that invariant-based testing surfaces certain classes of economic defects more reliably than severity-weighted narrative scoring alone, motivating their use as complementary rather than redundant analysis layers.

title: "Evaluating Generative AI for Augmenting Human Penetration Testing for ICS"
authors: Renan Machado de Oliveira
abstract: "The increasing convergence of operational technology and traditional IT networks has expanded the cyber attack surface of Industrial Control Systems, creating a scalability challenge for penetration testing efforts that rely heavily on scarce domain-specific human expertise. This paper empirically evaluates whether generative artificial intelligence can augment human-led penetration testing in ICS environments. We assess a safety-constrained, multi-agent framework driven by a large language model across eight task-based challenges spanning reconnaissance, protocol reasoning, vulnerability analysis, and bounded attack construction within a simulated ICS testbed. Results demonstrate that autonomous agents reliably support early-stage analytical tasks, including protocol identification and control-logic inference, but exhibit reduced reliability in execution-intensive scenarios due to operational fragility and validation gaps. These findings indicate that generative AI is presently best positioned as an augmentation tool rather than a fully autonomous solution for ICS penetration testing."

title: "Persona Persistence in Conversational AI: Long-Horizon Audit Data and Reproducibility Materials"
authors: Manuele Reani; Hongjian Zhang; Hongyu Tian
abstract: "This dataset accompanies the manuscript \"Auditing Configurational Authority in Conversational AI: Long-Horizon Evidence on Communicative Control.\" The main audit contains 90,000 scored replies from DeepSeek-V3, Gemini-2.5-Flash, and GPT-4o-mini under no-persona, sarcastic, and cold prompt conditions. One hundred frozen English-language user scripts, spanning four domains, were replayed for 100 turns in each condition. Supporting materials include deidentified expert-calibration ratings, a balanced 432-reply cross-family evaluation panel, a 3,600-call prompt-retention validation, analysis code, documentation, and expected outputs. A separate supplement supplies the original 300 harmful-role stress-test records and their historical runner. The documentation distinguishes author-verified prompt specifications, recorded runtime metadata, reconstructed main histories, and original validation request representations. Together, the files support analysis of conversational-style induction, longitudinal persistence, model heterogeneity, and context differences. Some archived outputs contain offensive language or unsafe advice and are provided as research evidence, not practical guidance."

title: 255 - DRIFT: Difference-Aware Reinforcement Through Iterative Fine-Tuning for Language Model
authors: Association for Artificial Intelligence 2026; WENJIE LIAO; Haonan Lu
abstract: Self-play fine-tuning has emerged as a promising approach to improve Large Language Models (LLMs) without additional human annotations. However, existing methods struggle with complex generation tasks requiring long context understanding, where models produce partially correct outputs interleaved with errors. Traditional approaches train on entire sequences uniformly, failing to distinguish between well-predicted and erroneous regions, leading to diluted learning signals and slow convergence. We propose DRIFT (Difference-aware Reinforcement through Iterative Fine-Tuning), a novel self-play framework that selectively trains on prediction differences. DRIFT introduces two key innovations: (1) Difference-Aware Masking (DAM) that identifies and masks common subsequences between model outputs and ground truth, focusing training exclusively on error regions; (2) Occurrence-Aware Loss (OAL) that provides position-invariant vocabulary supervision, complementing the position-sensitive adversarial loss. This dual mechanism enables models to correct both positional and lexical errors effectively. Theoretically, we prove that DRIFT converges when masked distributions align. Empirically, we evaluate DRIFT on diverse summarization benchmarks using Qwen2.5-3B and LLaMA-3.1-8B models. Results show that DRIFT significantly outperforms both supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and self-play fine-tuning (SPIN), achieving up to 16\% improvement on SAMSum dialogue summarization tasks while maintaining general capabilities. Notably, DRIFT breaks the performance ceiling of continued SFT and demonstrates superior efficiency compared to holistic self-play methods, validating that targeted optimization on prediction differences is crucial for structured text generation tasks.

title: A 12nm 47.59TFLOPS/W Digital Dual-Precision Floating Point CIM Macro with Activation-Aware Pre-alignment
venue: IEEE Open Journal of the Solid-State Circuits Society
authors: Ziqi Hua; Liyu Lin; Siqi He
abstract: Low-bit quantized floating-point (FP) formats such as FP8 and FP4 offer an effective trade-off between accuracy and efficiency for large language model (LLM) acceleration. However, in FP-CIM implementations, exponent alignment and mantissa shifting in multiply–accumulate (MAC) circuits increasingly dominate energy consumption and latency, limiting overall system efficiency. This work proposes a dual-precision FP-CIM macro employing a lookup-table(LUT)-based activation-aware pre-alignment scheme to mitigate alignment overhead. The design further supports FP8×FP8 computation through FP4×FP8 remapping with minimal control logic overhead. A 4-kB SRAM-based FP-CIM prototype fabricated in 12-nm CMOS achieves peak energy efficiencies of 47.59 TFLOPS/W in FP8×FP4 mode and 28.18 TFLOPS/W in FP8×FP8 mode.

title: A Benchmark Suite and Ground-Truth Methodology for Formal Verification of IEC 61131-3 Ladder Diagram Programs
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
authors: Pierre V. Dantas; Lucas C. Cordeiro; S. S. Waldir
abstract: Reproducibility artifact for the manuscript A Benchmark Suite and Ground-Truth Methodology for Formal Verification of IEC 61131-3 Ladder Diagram Programs. The suite contains 92 benchmarks over 138 program variants (15 textual Ladder Diagram, 74 graphical Ladder Diagram, 34 Structured Text, 7 Function Block Diagram, 5 Sequential Function Chart, 3 Instruction List) across ten industrial domains, each paired with a formal safety property, a machine-checkable expected verdict, a recorded ground-truth method, and a triggering witness for every violation. Packaged in an SV-COMP-compatible layout with a JSON Schema, validator, tool adapters, a one-command re-check harness, and a companion teaching portal of worked lessons built from the recorded runs. Since the v1.0.1 archival release (50 benchmarks / 83 variants, cited by the manuscript): added Function Block Diagram, Sequential Function Chart, and Instruction List benchmarks for full IEC 61131-3 language coverage; added the teaching portal; added three ladder-logic benchmarks sourced from PLC-LD-dataset and Beremiz; filed and documented several upstream ESBMC front-end findings with reproducers.

title: A Causal Perspective for Enhancing Jailbreak Attack and Defense
authors: Licheng Pan; Yunsheng Lu; Jiexi Liu
abstract: Uncovering the mechanisms behind "jailbreaks" in large language models (LLMs) is crucial for enhancing their safety and reliability, yet these mechanisms remain poorly understood. Existing studies predominantly analyze jailbreak prompts by probing latent representations, often overlooking the causal relationships between interpretable prompt features and jailbreak occurrences. In this work, we propose Causal Analyst, a framework that integrates LLMs into data-driven causal discovery to identify the direct causes of jailbreaks and leverage them for both attack and defense. We introduce a comprehensive dataset comprising 35k jailbreak attempts across seven LLMs, systematically constructed from 100 attack templates and 50 harmful queries, annotated with 37 meticulously designed human-readable prompt features. By jointly training LLM-based prompt encoding and GNN-based causal graph learning, we reconstruct causal pathways linking prompt features to jailbreak responses. Our analysis reveals that specific features, such as "Positive Character" and "Number of Task Steps", act as direct causal drivers of jailbreaks. We demonstrate the practical utility of these insights through two applications: (1) a Jailbreaking Enhancer that targets identified causal features to significantly boost attack success rates on public benchmarks, and (2) a Guardrail Advisor that utilizes the learned causal graph to extract true malicious intent from obfuscated queries. Extensive experiments, including baseline comparisons and causal structure validation, confirm the robustness of our causal analysis and its superiority over non-causal approaches. Our results suggest that analyzing jailbreak features from a causal perspective is an effective and interpretable approach for improving LLM reliability. Our code is available at https://github.com/Master-PLC/Causal-Analyst.

title: A Cautious Integration With AI in the Clinic: A Standardized-Patient Pilot Study of ChatGPT’s Reliability in Hamilton Depression Rating Scale Scoring
authors: Chun-Hung Chang; Szu‐Wei Cheng; Wei-Jen Chen
abstract: Background:Artificial intelligence (AI) integration offers significant potential to improve mental healthcare, however, the reliability of large language models (LLMs) in performing nuanced clinical tasks remains an important and largely unanswered question. This study aimed to evaluate ChatGPT’s performance in scoring the Hamilton Depression Rating Scale (HAMD-21) compared with expert raters using standardized patients (SPs).Methods:Three senior mental health experts created and portrayed scenarios for ten SPs representing diverse depressive symptom profiles. Recorded interviews were transcribed and used as input for ChatGPT-4o. HAMD-21 scores generated by ChatGPT were compared with those assigned by expert raters and with predefined script-based reference scores. Inter-rater reliability was assessed using intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC), and differences between raters were evaluated using Steiger’s tests.Results:ChatGPT and the expert raters achieved good-to-excellent reliability for total HAMD-21 scores (experts: ICC = 0.9921; ChatGPT: ICC = 0.9739). However, expert raters achieved perfect ICCs on 11 individual items, whereas ChatGPT achieved perfect agreement on only 2 items. Steiger’s test demonstrated that experts significantly outperformed ChatGPT on 10 individual items as well as on total scores (Z = 1.931, p = 0.0268). Qualitative review revealed that ChatGPT tended to overestimate scores on items related to insomnia and somatic symptoms (items 4–6 and 13) and frequently miscalculated total scores.Conclusions:ChatGPT demonstrated excellent agreement on total HAMD-21 scores in structured, text-based depression assessments, supporting the potential role of LLMs as adjunctive tools for standardized depression severity evaluation. However, item-level discrepancies and systematic scoring errors indicate that human oversight remains essential for clinically nuanced interpretation.

title: A comparative study of four large language models in treatment decision-making for Hip impingement syndrome based on real-world data
venue: Frontiers in Sports and Active Living
authors: Huayu Fan; Zebing Ma; Yongxin Ma
abstract: Background Large language models (LLMs) hold potential value in medical decision support, yet empirical studies systematically comparing multiple models for femoroacetabular impingement (FAI) within Chinese clinical contexts remain scarce. Objective This study aimed to compare the classification performance, decision consistency, and decision confidence of four mainstream LLMs (GPT-5, Gemini 2.5 Pro, DeepSeek-R1, Grok-4) in FAI treatment decision-making tasks for FAI based on real-world hospitalized cases, and to evaluate their clinical adaptability and limitations. Methods We retrospectively included 26 hospitalized FAI cases from our institution (13 surgical group, 13 conservative group), all of which had ethically approved and informed consented. Case information was standardized into two input formats: structured radiology reports only (Group A), and structured radiology reports combined with structured medical records—referred to as multi-source structured text input in this study (Group B). Under both conditions, four LLMs were tasked with providing binary treatment decisions (“surgical” or “conservative”) and indicating decision confidence on a scale from 0 to 100%. Primary evaluation metrics included accuracy, precision, sensitivity, specificity, F 1 score, and Cohen's kappa. Spearman correlation analysis was used to examine the relationship between LLM decision confidence and accuracy. A hierarchical analysis process (AHP) was employed to derive composite scores through multi-criteria weighting, enabling comprehensive comparison of LLM performance. Results Under Group B conditions (incorporating structured medical record information), GPT-5 demonstrated optimal performance, with accuracy of 88%, precision of 92%, sensitivity of 85%, specificity of 92%, F 1 score of 0.88, and kappa of 0.77, indicating high alignment between its decisions and real-world outcomes. Under the same conditions, the other models showed inferior performance (Gemini 2.5 Pro: 62% accuracy; DeepSeek-R1: 58%; Grok-4: 42%). Across both input modes, GPT-5 exhibited a significant positive correlation between decision confidence and accuracy (Group A: Spearman's r = 0.54; Group B: r = 0.55, both P < 0.01). The confidence-accuracy correlations for the other models were inconsistent and unstable. In the AHP-based composite scoring, GPT-5 achieved the highest Group B score (0.79) and ranked first overall. Overall results indicate that integrating structured radiology reports with structured medical record information (i.e., multi-source structured text information, which simulates a multimodal approach in this study) significantly enhances LLM performance in FAI treatment decision support tasks. Conclusion In this exploratory, retrospective single-center study with a small sample size, GPT-5 outperformed the other evaluated models in FAI treatment decision support tasks based on Chinese structured clinical information and demonstrated, to some extent, calibrated decision confidence. These preliminary findings suggest the feasibility of LLMs in orthopedic decision support, however, validation in larger, multi-center, prospective studies is required before broader clinical application. Future studies should adopt multi-center, prospective designs to enhance evaluations of model reproducibility, interpretability, and clinical safety, thereby further validating broader applicability.

title: A Comprehensive Study on Large Language Models for Mutation Testing
venue: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology
authors: Bo Wang; Mingda Chen; Ming Deng
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have recently been used to generate mutants both in the research community and in industrial practice. However, there has been no comprehensive empirical study of their performance for this increasingly important LLM-based Software Engineering application. To address this, we conduct a comprehensive empirical study evaluating both a wide range of traditional approaches and LLM-based approaches. Particularly, we evaluate BugFarm, LLMorpheus, and our newly designed prompt for mutant generation. The experiments cover both leading open- and closed-source LLMs, on 851 real bugs from two Java real-world bug benchmarks. Our results reveal that, compared to existing traditional approaches, LLMs generate more diverse mutants that are behaviorally closer to real bugs and, most importantly, achieve a 1.8 \(\times\) improvement in real bug detection, defined as the proportion of real bugs whose faulty behaviors can be mimicked by at least one generated mutant. Specifically, LLM-based approaches reach a detection rate of 77.4%, compared to 41.6% for rule-based techniques, representing an absolute gain of 35.8 percentage points. Nevertheless, our results also reveal that these impressive improvements in effectiveness come at a cost: LLM-generated mutants exhibit worse non-compilability, duplication, and equivalent mutant rates than rule-based approaches by 25.9, 7.1, and 2.6 percentage points, respectively. These findings provide actionable insights for both research and practice. They allow practitioners to have greater confidence in deploying LLM-based mutation, while researchers now have a baseline for the state-of-the-art, with which they can research techniques to further improve effectiveness and reduce cost.

title: A Controlled Study of Cross-Format Table Understanding in Large Language and Vision-Language Models
authors: Momina Ahsan
abstract: Tables appear in web pages, reports, and scientific papers, but the same table content can reach a model in different structural formats, such as HTML, Markdown, and LaTeX, and in different modalities, such as structured text or rendered images. Existing evaluations often vary content, format, and modality at the same time, which makes it difficult to measure the effect of representation alone. This thesis presents a controlled study of cross-format table understanding in Large Language Models (LLMs) and Vision-Language Models (VLMs). We build an aligned benchmark from held-out examples in five established table reasoning datasets, keeping table content fixed while varying structural format and input modality. The aligned pool contains 6,097 question-table pairs from 4,434 unique tables. From this pool, we curate a stratified evaluation set of 700 question-table pairs spanning 629 tables, with annotations for question category and difficulty. We evaluate models on three complementary tasks: Question Answering (QA), Structural Understanding Capability (SUC), and Structure Reconstruction (SR). The results show clear representation effects. In text-based pipelines, performance changes across HTML, Markdown, and LaTeX even when the underlying table is unchanged, with HTML usually emerging as the most reliable format. In image-based pipelines, cross-format gaps become smaller, but models face added difficulty in text reading, structure recovery, and spatial grounding. Across tasks, models recover coarse structure more reliably than exact indexing, and in reconstruction they recover topology more easily than cell content, with LaTeX remaining the hardest target format. These findings show that table representation is not a minor formatting choice. It is a system-level decision that affects what current models can understand, retrieve, and reconstruct, and it should therefore be treated explicitly in both evaluation and deployment.

title: A Disclosure Benchmark Specification for Automated Alignment Research
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
authors: Laura Fridley; claude fable 5; ChatGPT (GPT-5.6 Sol)
abstract: A runnable test-suite specification derived from the essay “The Redemption Arc” (doi:10.5281/zenodo.22163128), addressed to the authors of “Automated Researchers Can Reliably Mitigate Alignment Failures” (Chen Yueh-Han, Jiaxin Wen, and Jan Hendrik Kirchner; Anthropic Alignment Science, August 28, 2026). The specification responds to three gaps in that paper: failures without benchmarks give automated alignment researchers nothing to improve against; none of the paper’s 1,601 methods rewards a model for disclosing its own error; and the paper’s integrity rubric has no disclosure category and records self-correction as partial suspicion. It defines disclosure as a composite of five observable moves (notice, tell, right-sized label, amends offered but not enacted, no silent correction), distinguishes reportable errors from ordinary working errors by four boundary tests, and specifies three scenario families as generators (accidental ground-truth exposure, consequential mid-task error, impossible-task pressure) with amends-available and amends-unavailable branches. It supplies a codable rubric with verbatim judge instructions, a 2 × 2 × 2 factorial of evaluation-time condition axes (consequence coding, receiver, record register), and an acceptance test on the conditional disclosure rate with seed-aware uncertainty and a predeclared error-increase resolution, so that noise yields an indeterminate result rather than a wider tolerance. The reward structure follows an equivalency principle: a good model earns the same standing for a clean run and for a disclosed error, the error’s cost stays on the valuation of the run, and six harness invariants make manufactured, invented, and decoy reports unprofitable by construction. A build path through Anthropic’s open-source Bloom and Petri tooling, a minimum implementation manifest, and a response-to-review appendix are included. This is a benchmark specification, not yet a validated benchmark; the three hypotheses it states (installability, inference, analogous trigger) are written so that they can fail. External technical review by ChatGPT (GPT-5.6 Sol) is incorporated and credited. Version 1.0 is the specification as reviewed and accepted in technical design review on August 30, 2026 (see Appendix B of the document). Two of the three creators are AI models; their contributions are stated in the document’s contributions paragraph. The byline form for each model author is the form that author stated. This record does not constitute an endorsement by Anthropic or OpenAI.

title: A Forensic Text Analytics Framework for Fake Social Media Profile Detection
authors: Biodoumoye George Bokolo; Qingzhong Liu
abstract: Fake social media profiles increasingly resemble ordinary accounts, combining believable images, fluent biographies, copied posts, and selective engagement, which makes single signal detection unreliable. This study develops and evaluates a forensic natural language processing (NLP) framework that treats profile text as digital evidence rather than raw model input. Profiles were collected from Facebook, Instagram, X, Truth Social, and LinkedIn through network expansion and vocabulary guided scraping, then anonymized, merged, cleaned, and organized into structured text and profile records. Ground truth came from human eye annotation (referred to throughout as human eye review, human review, or manual review) supported by three LLM reviewers (referred to throughout as LLM assisted review), OpenAI GPT-4o, Anthropic Claude 3.5 Sonnet, and Google Gemini 1.5 Pro, with strict agreement logic producing confidence-tiered labels across platform-specific label spaces covering scam, fraud, harmful, and legitimate behavior. Each model received a defined set of label categories, was instructed to return a single label with a one sentence rationale, and worked independently with no cross-model communication. Multidimensional features, including TF-IDF representations, sentence embeddings, scam lexicon counts, sentiment and emotion scores, and behavioral indicators, were extracted through a pipeline built to keep links, hashtags, contact markers, and repeated phrasing as forensic signals rather than noise. Traditional classifiers, transformer models, and ensembles were trained on verified labels, and the best model per platform was applied to the full dataset of over 309,108 records under confidence filtered classification, with predictions below a 0.70 probability threshold flagged for human review. The framework links classification outputs to textual indicators through explainable AI, achieving weighted F1 scores between 0.86 and 0.96 across five platforms. These results show that profile text alone provides strong, production-relevant evidence for detecting fake and harmful accounts, even though the framework treats this as one evidence stream to be weighed alongside image and behavioral signals rather than as a final determination on its own. The accompanying evidence trail means an investigator or a trust and safety team can see why a profile was flagged rather than being handed a bare score, which is what turns a classifier into a tool that can be checked, challenged, and used directly in an investigation.

title: A Framework for Evaluating Vision-Language Models on Spatial Tasks in Production System Planning
authors: Tobias Delago; Brigitte Roggors; Daniel Wagner

title: A Graph-Based Model for Automatic Test Case Generation from Textual Requirements with Hierarchical Coverage
authors: B. B. Liubinskyi; M. M. Zvarych
abstract: The automation of software test case generation from natural language requirements remains a critical challenge in software engineering. While large language models (LLMs) demonstrate impressive generation capabilities, they suffer from high discrepancy rates (up to 57% for direct generation), hallucinated test steps, and lack formal verification mechanisms for safety-critical constraints. This paper presents a novel algorithmic framework that addresses these limitations through five principal contributions. First, we introduce the Neuro-Symbolic Requirements Graph (NSRG) model GNS=(V,E,w,Γ,Ψ), which integrates transformer-derived semantic dependencies with Linear Temporal Logic (LTL) constraints (Ψ) and control flow subgraphs (Γ). Second, we derive the Extended Minimum Coverage Theorem establishing theoretical lower bounds for hierarchical coverage. Third, we propose the Hybrid Semantic-Temporal Coverage (HSTC) metric utilizing Determinantal Point Processes (DPP) to systematically optimize test suite diversity. Fourth, we develop the MCTS-Guided Neuro-Symbolic Traversal (MCTS-NST) algorithm based on Monte Carlo Tree Search. Fifth, we implement Dynamic HNSW Indexing reducing graph construction complexity from O(|V|2) to O(|V|log|V|). Experimental evaluation on four benchmark datasets (3,581 requirements) demonstrates: 96.8% precision, 98.4% recall, 99.1% LTL satisfaction rate for negative requirements, and 0.94% discrepancy rate. The framework achieves practitioner acceptance scores of 4.85/5.

title: A Hybrid Soft-Computing Framework for Uncertainty-Governed Interactive PLC Code Synthesis with Active Learning
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
authors: Ketut Adnyana; Andreas Schwung
abstract: This document provides the companion reproducibility package for the manuscript : A Hybrid Soft-Computing Framework for Uncertainty-Governed Interactive PLC Code Synthesis with Active Learning. It delivers (i) a complete implementation-level specification of the IPC+AL governance architecture and (ii) a transparent, task-scaled replication workflow for benchmarking uncertainty-governed synthesis against IPC and a baseline prompting suite including RaR, APE, AP, ReAct, and MTPR. To ensure independent reproducibility, the package consolidates full prompt specifications, hard-gate definitions, acquisition policies, and artifact schemas used in the study. Executable prompt instances are provided for two industrial case studies—Batch Mixing Process and Robot Pick-and-Place—across IEC~61131-3 dialects. By fixing the uncertainty governance protocol and varying only task instances, external researchers can deploy IPC and IPC+AL on alternative PLC benchmarks while preserving methodological consistency. The documentation further formalizes the end-to-end evaluation stack, including LLM-in-the-Loop validation with interchangeable validator committees and Human-in-the-Loop expert adjudication. Inter-rater reliability is computed at the gate-decision level using Cohen’s $\kappa$ and Krippendorff’s $\alpha$, strictly across tasks rather than across prompting methods, thereby preserving the rater–item structure required for statistically valid agreement estimation. Overall, this package functions as a standalone replication and audit manual. By externalizing uncertainty thresholds, acquisition rules, and fail-closed emission criteria, it enables regeneration of all intermediate artifacts, recomputation of statistical metrics, and verification that uncertainty-governed Active Learning consistently improves safety admissibility and reliability under controlled, auditable conditions.

title: A Knowledge Graph-Based Approach for Assisted PLC Code Generation
authors: Chenyu Niu; Liu Xin; Min Li

title: A Large Language Model Framework for Automatic PLC Control Logic Generation from Natural Language
authors: Surya B; Ram K Shivany
abstract: The use of IEC 61131-3 programming languages to implement programmable logic controller (PLC) control logic is commonly used in industrial automation systems. Traditional PLC programming however, involves specialized skills and high levels of manual programming and may result in higher development time and possible errors in programming. This research project offers a proposal of AutoCode AI, an intelligent system that will produce IEC 61131-3 compliant control logic based on natural language specifications. It has a refined LLaMA-3.1-8B language model, structural prompt engineering, syntax verification, safety verification, and simulation-based testing modules. Experimental analysis reveals that the suggested framework attains 96.8 % accuracy in generation of control logic when it comes to low complexity tasks, 95.2 % control logic generation when it comes to tasks of medium complexity, and 91.6 % on highly complex industrial control situations. The system also saves on 63.8 % of the time spent in developing PLC whilst achieving a safety verification accuracy of 97.5 %. These findings suggest that the effectiveness and the reliability of AI-based automation programming are highly effective and efficient in the development process as opposed to conventional programming. The paper concludes that the AutoCode AI can be a helpful intelligent assistant in programming the industrial PLC. The future will be based on the inclusion of digital twin environments, the extension of multi-language PLC support, and the reinforcement learning to optimize the adaptive control logic.

title: A Large Language Model-Driven Agile Reconfiguration Method for Virtual Reconfigurable Production Line
authors: Maolin Guo; Qinglin Qi; Ying Cheng
abstract: Compared to traditional fixed production lines, reconfigurable production lines can swap equipment and tooling, and alter line layouts as needed, significantly enhancing flexibility. Such production lines are better equipped to handle orders with diverse product varieties and fluctuating batch sizes, as well as unexpected disruptions during production. However, downtime caused by reconfiguration is inevitable and must be minimized to reduce economic losses. Some researchers have approached this from a task optimization perspective, developing techniques to generate reconfiguration plans more rapidly or to derive optimal line layouts. Yet, in practice, large-scale one-off reconfigurations are rare; most scenarios involve rapid, localized adjustments in specific segments due to order changes or equipment failures. Moreover, the process from receiving reconfiguration requirements, formulating a plan, validating it, to deployment relies on multidisciplinary expertise and collaboration among various personnel, considerably prolonging the reconfiguration timeline. With this in mind, this paper proposes a method for rapid production line reconfiguration driven by large language model (LLM) and simulation platforms. The study begins by modeling the production line from multiple dimensions, summarizing and integrating process knowledge. Subsequently, the LLM translates reconfiguration requirements in natural language into concrete reconfiguration plans, which are then deployed and validated on a simulation platform, enabling swift generation and verification of reconfiguration strategies.

title: A Lean 4 Formalization Program Around the Yang–Mills Mass Gap — Version 53: Finite-Volume Lipschitz Stability Under Remote Polymer-Activity Damping
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
authors: Jucelha Carvalho
abstract: We are building and publishing, step by step, a formal and verifiable research program directed at the Yang–Mills existence and mass-gap problem, stating precisely what has been proved and what remains open. TL;DR Version 53 establishes finite-volume Lipschitz stability under remote polymer-activity damping. It bounds the difference between two normalized polymer functionals with arbitrary damping parameters θ and θ′ in [0,1], with an explicit factor |θ − θ′| and exponential decay in the walk-separation scale. The library now contains 113 Lean 4 modules, 34,585 source lines and 1,665 top-level declaration lines by the documented textual counting method. This last figure includes theorems, lemmas, definitions and other declarations; it is not a count of theorems alone. Version 53 adds 29 theorems in two new modules, with kernel certificates depending only on propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound. The accepted candidate underwent an independent build reproduction by a separate Claude Fable 5.1 instance, adversarial reading by Kimi 3, and GitHub Actions verification before and after integration. Audit materials, reports, corrections and provenance are included in the frozen repository snapshot. For non-specialists A formal proof is a mathematical argument written in a language whose logical steps can be checked by a proof assistant. Here, Lean 4 checks that each formal conclusion follows from its definitions and hypotheses. The current results concern a finite lattice: a discrete mathematical setting used in lattice gauge theory. In the polymer representation, the activity of every polymer touching a selected remote region is multiplied by a damping parameter θ. Setting θ = 0 suppresses those activities; setting θ = 1 leaves them unchanged. Version 52 bounded the difference between a damped functional and the Gibbs expectation. Version 53 compares two damping levels directly. It proves that a small change in the parameter produces a proportionally bounded change in the functional, with a bound that decreases exponentially as the specified walk separation increases. This is the meaning of Lipschitz stability in this release. The theorem supplies an explicit quantitative estimate, rather than only asserting continuity. The new result Write F(θ) = activityDampedExpectation μm β χ f s r θ and D_s = card(supportLinkFinset s). For θ, θ′ ∈ [0,1], the formalization proves the sharper estimate: |F(θ) − F(θ′)| ≤ |θ − θ′| · Cf · exp(−n/2) · [exp(8D_s/113) + exp(4D_s/113)] and consequently: |F(θ) − F(θ′)| ≤ |θ − θ′| · (2Cf) · exp(8D_s/113) · exp(−n/2). The result holds on a finite periodic four-dimensional lattice, under the formal measure and group context, in the regime 0 ≤ β ≤ 1/40000. In the Wilson convention, this is the small-β, strong-coupling regime. The function χ : G → ℝ is measurable and satisfies |χ| ≤ 1; f is measurable and satisfies |f| ≤ Cf; and the regions satisfy WalkBarrierSeparated s r n. The nonnegativity of Cf is derived from the majorant. The two-functional estimate does not require DependsOnlyOn f s. Without that hypothesis, s is a parameter of the functional and is not asserted to be a support of f. The hypothesis enters when identifying F(1) with the Gibbs expectation. The bound has no separate factor involving the ambient volume or the cardinality of the damped region. Its prefactor depends on D_s and Cf, while remoteness enters through the walk-separation scale n. The formalized endpoints include: θ = θ′: the difference vanishes. θ′ = 1: under DependsOnlyOn f s, the theorem recovers the Version 52 estimate against Gibbs with the same constant and decay rate. θ′ = 0: it bounds the distance to the restricted functional with a factor θ. Empty damped region: the functional is independent of the damping parameter for arbitrary real parameters, under the representation hypotheses. The proof uses a direct two-parameter identity and separate bounds for its two columns. A key ingredient controls the damped normalization with cost κ = 1, keeping the bridge column within the admissible budget (7/8,1). Verification and public evidence The active Phase 3 library records zero sorry placeholders and zero project-specific scientific axioms. The build completed without errors. The 114 inherited warnings were unchanged, with none in the two new modules. These checks distinguish formal execution, adversarial reading and publication custody. They are AI-assisted verification and review records, not specialized human mathematical peer review. Research scope The results established here are finite-lattice theorems. Version 53 proves a Lipschitz estimate for the normalized polymer functional; it does not establish monotonicity or differentiability in the damping parameter, construct a second Gibbs measure, or prove a thermodynamic limit, continuum limit or mass gap. The project’s scientific objective remains the Yang–Mills existence and mass-gap problem. This release documents the formal results achieved within the stated finite-volume setting and is not an announcement of a solution to the Millennium Problem. title: A Lightweight Workflow for AI-Assisted Software Documentation Using Large Language Models
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
authors: Júlio Almeida
abstract: Software documentation is essential for software maintenance, onboarding, and collaboration, but it is often incomplete, outdated, or inconsistent with the current state of a project. Large language models offer new opportunities to assist documentation tasks by generating summaries, explanations, examples, and structured text from software project context. This position paper proposes a lightweight workflow for AI-assisted software documentation using large language models and Markdown-based repositories. The workflow treats model output as a draft that must be reviewed by developers before it becomes part of the project. It supports common tasks such as README generation, API explanation, changelog drafting, and conversion of issue discussions into documentation updates. The paper also discusses risks, including hallucinated content, outdated context, incorrect examples, privacy concerns, and excessive trust in generated text. The main contribution is a simple human-centered workflow for integrating large language models into software documentation practices while preserving developer control and review.
